issues.legal_issue: A divorced woman who has not remarried may qualify for maintenance under the criminal procedure code if she otherwise meets the statutory conditions.
material_facts: The husband divorced the woman, and she later sought maintenance for herself and her child.
She was in financial difficulty and unable to maintain herself.
The trial court granted her maintenance, but the lower appellate courts rejected her claim on the ground that she was divorced.
issues.conclusion: Divorce does not by itself remove an otherwise eligible, non-remarried woman from the class entitled to maintenance.
issues.legal_principle: Section 125(1), Explanation (b), of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, includes a woman divorced by or obtaining a divorce from her husband, if she has not remarried, within the meaning of “wife.” The provision is to be read purposively as a welfare measure, informed by Articles 15(3), 38 and 39 of the Constitution; Article 37 identifies the Directive Principles as fundamental to governance. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.divorced_woman_support_case: A woman who has been divorced seeks maintenance from her former husband.
predicates.woman_not_remarried: The divorced woman has not remarried.
predicates.woman_unable_to_support_herself: The woman is unable to maintain herself.

issues.definition: If a non-remarried divorced woman seeks support from her former husband and cannot maintain herself, she is eligible for maintenance.

issues.legal_issue: A husband’s divorce of his wife and provision of a separate residence can establish that the statutory bar concerning spouses living separately by mutual consent does not defeat a divorced woman’s maintenance claim.
material_facts: The husband divorced the woman and provided for her to live separately, as reflected in the settlement concerning the residence.
The woman later sought maintenance from him.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances supported the conclusion that the woman was not living separately by mutual consent, so the mutual-consent bar did not defeat her claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 125(4) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, addresses the bar to maintenance when spouses live separately by mutual consent. The Court held that a husband’s divorce of his wife, together with his provision of a separate residence, can establish the relevant circumstances without requiring separate proof negating mutual consent. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.divorced_woman_support_case: A divorced woman seeks maintenance from her former husband.
predicates.husband_provided_separate_residence: The husband provided the woman with a separate residence.

issues.definition: When a husband divorces a woman seeking maintenance and provides her a separate residence, those facts prevent the mutual-consent bar from defeating her claim.

issues.legal_issue: A husband’s denial of an obligation to support a divorced woman, without evidence that he has been providing her support, satisfies the neglect requirement for maintenance.
material_facts: The woman sought maintenance because she was unable to maintain herself.
The husband argued that she had no maintenance claim because she was divorced and had settled her claims.
The husband did not give evidence that he had been providing her with allowances.
issues.conclusion: The neglect requirement was satisfied because the husband’s position was that he could ignore the woman’s claim, and he offered no evidence of support.
issues.legal_principle: Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, requires neglect or refusal to maintain. The Court assessed the circumstances broadly, noting the husband’s denial of any obligation and the absence of evidence that he had been supporting the woman. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.divorced_woman_support_case: A divorced woman seeks maintenance from her former husband.
predicates.husband_denied_support_obligation: The husband asserts that he has no obligation to support the woman.
predicates.no_support_payments_proved: The husband does not prove that he has been providing support to the woman.

issues.definition: In a divorced woman’s maintenance case, a husband’s denial of any support obligation and the absence of proof of support satisfy the neglect requirement.

issues.legal_issue: A settlement made before a statutory maintenance right existed does not waive or defeat that later-created right.
material_facts: The parties entered into a consent decree settling their then-existing disputes and claims.
The decree stated that the woman had no further claim or right against the husband.
The decree preceded the later statutory right on which the woman based her maintenance claim.
issues.conclusion: The earlier consent decree could not negate the woman’s later statutory maintenance claim.
issues.legal_principle: Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, created a statutory right that was not available when the earlier settlement was made. A settlement of claims then available cannot operate to extinguish that later statutory right. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.divorced_woman_support_case: A divorced woman seeks maintenance from her former husband under a statutory right.
predicates.settlement_predates_statutory_right: The parties settled their claims before the statutory maintenance right existed.
predicates.settlement_purports_to_resolve_claims: The earlier settlement purports to resolve the parties’ claims against one another.

issues.definition: An earlier settlement that purports to resolve claims does not bar a divorced woman’s statutory maintenance claim when the settlement predates that right.

issues.legal_issue: A customary or personal-law payment on divorce relieves a husband of the obligation to provide maintenance only if the payment is reasonably sufficient to serve as a substitute for maintenance.
material_facts: The husband relied on a payment made on divorce and the settlement recording the parties’ financial arrangements to argue that no maintenance remained payable.
The payment identified as mehar was Rs. 5,000, with Rs. 180 identified as iddat money.
The Court found the mehar amount inadequate to provide for the woman’s maintenance.
issues.conclusion: The payment did not extinguish the husband’s maintenance obligation because it was not a reasonable substitute for maintenance; an inadequate payment may affect the maintenance rate but does not eliminate it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 127(3)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, permits cancellation of a maintenance order in the specified circumstances where a divorced woman has received the sum payable on divorce under applicable customary or personal law. Read with Section 125 and the social purpose of Chapter IX, the payment must have a rational relation to the woman’s maintenance needs and be reasonably sufficient to serve as a substitute for maintenance. An illusory payment may reduce the maintenance rate but cannot annihilate it. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.divorced_woman_support_case: A divorced woman seeks maintenance from her former husband.
predicates.customary_or_personal_law_payment_receiv: The woman received a payment on divorce under a customary or personal-law arrangement.
predicates.payment_not_reasonably_sufficient_for_ma: The payment is not reasonably sufficient to provide for the woman’s maintenance.

issues.definition: In a divorced woman’s maintenance case, a payment received on divorce does not extinguish the support obligation if it is not reasonably sufficient to provide for her maintenance.
